record.label: No bounded gap between support points
record.statement: For an admissible minimizer gamma and its Stieltjes measure, no support-free interval (a,b) can have endpoints a,b in S with 0<=a<b<1. Constancy of gamma and contact give q(a)=a, q(b)=b and q'(a),q'(b)<=1. If the plateau height is positive, strict convexity gives q'(t) below the endpoint chord and below 1; if zero, strict increase gives q'(t)<q'(b)<=1. Integration contradicts q(b)-q(a)=b-a.
record.boundary: Curated source-level mathematical statement, not an elaborated Lean extraction or independently accepted proof. Its displayed local hypotheses are quantified guards; a hypothetical plateau is not an added premise of the full-support theorem. Includes a=0 only when 0 lies in the support, using the one-sided slope bound there. All q and gamma occurrences refer to the same diffusion/coefficient. A schematic area illustration is not a prerequisite. The minimizer premise here belongs to the ordinary manuscript model; formal-interface hypotheses remain on the separate Lean target. This classification does not prove a transport between formal models.

aligned_passages.text: **Theorem 5.1 (full support).** In the pure zero-field SK model with $\xi(t)=t^2/2$, let $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ minimize $\mathcal P$. Then $\operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma=[0,1)$ and $\gamma$ is strictly increasing. For every associated diffusion started at zero, $\mathbb E u(t,X_t)^2=t$ and $\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^2=1$ for $0\le t<1$. Keep the same minimiser, diffusion and moment function $q$ throughout. Section 3 has established $G\ge0$, $G=0$ on the support $S=\operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma$, and the contact conditions $q(s)=s$, $q'(s)\le1$ at support points. At zero, the value identity comes from symmetry, and the slope bound requires $0\in S$. Section 4 supplies curvature on constant intervals for every admissible coefficient. These premises are available before any support gap is excluded. We first deal with the endpoint at one, then use the curvature estimate on the remaining intervals. For a terminal interval $(a,1)$, including empty support $[0,1)$, the cusp estimate gives $1-q(t)\gtrsim\sqrt{1-t}$ and hence $G<0$ near one. On a positive plateau with two contact endpoints, strict convexity puts $q'$ below its endpoint chord, although its integral must equal the interval length. On a zero plateau the heat argument makes $q'$ strictly increasing, below the right contact slope. At an initial gap, use the one-sided contact slope if $0\in S$; otherwise the coefficient is zero and symmetry supplies $q(0)=0$. **Why a terminal plateau violates the variational inequality.** Suppose that $\gamma=c$ on $(a,1)$, where $0\le a<1$ and $c\ge0$ is finite. The endpoint $1$ is outside the support domain, so there is no contact condition there to complete an endpoint-chord argument. Instead we will prove $$ 1-q(t)\ge C\sqrt{1-t} \tag{5.1} $$ for some $C>0$ and every $t$ sufficiently close to one. The proof separates two facts: the diffusion puts positive probability density near zero, and the smoothed terminal slope has a definite deficit from $\pm1$ in a shrinking window around zero. Fix $s\in(a,1)$ and let $\rho_s$ be the law of $X_s$. Choose $R<\infty$ such that $p_0=\rho_s([-R,R])>0$. For $c>0$, set $$ h(t,y)=\mathbb E e^{c|y+\sqrt{1-t}Z|},\qquad \Phi(t,y)=c^{-1}\log h(t,y), $$ where $Z$ is standard normal. The drift on this interval is $c\Phi_x=h_x/h$, and the transition density is $$ k_{s,t}(x,y)=p_{t-s}(y-x)\frac{h(t,y)}{h(s,x)},\qquad p_v(z)=(2\pi v)^{-1/2}e^{-z^2/(2v)}. \tag{5.2} $$ The heat-semigroup identity normalises this kernel; equivalently, for Brownian motion started at $(s,x)$, $h(t,B_t)/h(s,x)$ is the positive mean-one change of measure which adds the drift $h_x/h$. For $c=0$, the same kernel formula applies with $h=1$, and the value function is the ordinary heat evolution of $|x|$. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.3, proof of (6.6)][fs-var]. Put $L=1-s$ and $\delta=L/2$. For $s+\delta\le t<1$, $|x|\le R$ and $|y|\le1$, $$ p_{t-s}(y-x)\ge (2\pi L)^{-1/2}e^{-(R+1)^2/(2\delta)}=:k_*>0, $$ while $h(t,y)\ge1$ and $h(s,x)\le e^{cR}\mathbb E e^{c\sqrt L|Z|}=:M<\infty$. Integrating (5.2) over the part of $\rho_s$ in $[-R,R]$ therefore gives a density $f_t$ of $X_t$ with $$ f_t(y)\ge p_0k_*/M=:m>0 \quad(s+\delta\le t<1,\ |y|\le1). \tag{5.3} $$ Only positive mass of a compact set was needed at time $s$; no density assumption on $\rho_s$ has entered. Now write $\varepsilon=1-t$ and restrict to $|y|\le\sqrt\varepsilon$. Differentiating the terminal heat formula gives, with the unweighted interpretation for $c=0$, $$ u(t,y)= \frac{\mathbb E[\operatorname{sgn}(y+\sqrt\varepsilon Z) e^{c|y+\sqrt\varepsilon Z|}]} {\mathbb E e^{c|y+\sqrt\varepsilon Z|}}. $$ The denominator is at most $D=e^c\mathbb E e^{c|Z|}<\infty$. Each sign has unnormalised mass at least $p_*:=\mathbb P(Z\ge1)>0$: the threshold $|y/\sqrt\varepsilon|$ is at most one, and the exponential weight is at least one. Hence each sign has tilted probability at least $\theta=p_*/D\in(0,1/2)$. It follows that $$ |u(t,y)|\le1-2\theta,\qquad 1-u(t,y)^2\ge4\theta(1-\theta)=:\kappa>0. $$ Multiplying this uniform deficit by the density lower bound (5.3) and the window width $2\sqrt\varepsilon$ yields $$ 1-q(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}(1-u(t,y)^2)f_t(y)\,dy \ge 2m\kappa\sqrt{1-t}. $$ This proves (5.1) with $C=2m\kappa$. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.3, density and terminal-window estimates][fs-var]. The sign of the contradiction is now explicit. For $s'$ sufficiently close to one, the estimate holds at every $t\in[s',1)$, so $$ \begin{aligned} G(s')&=\int_{s'}^1(q(t)-t)\,dt\\ &\le\frac{(1-s')^2}{2} -\frac{2C}{3}(1-s')^{3/2}<0. \end{aligned} $$ The final inequality holds once $\sqrt{1-s'}<4C/3$. It contradicts the nonnegative cost of adding an atom at $s'$. This proof covers $c=0$ as well as $c>0$. In particular, empty support is impossible: then $\mu_\gamma=0$ and $\gamma=0$ on all of $[0,1)$. The terminal-plateau conclusion was already recorded in [Auffinger, Chen and Zeng (2020), Remark 7][acz]; the estimates above supply the quantitative argument needed here. **A shorter qualitative exclusion.** The existing curvature input also excludes a terminal support gap without estimating its boundary layer. Here is the elementary calculus step. Suppose $q\in C^1([r,1))$, $q(r)=r$, $q'(r)\le1$, $q\le1$, and $q'$ is strictly convex on $(r,1)$. If $q(t)\ge t$ at some $r1$. Compact-strip regularity gives continuity of $q'$ on $[a,b]$, even if $\gamma$ jumps at an endpoint. Contact gives $$ q(a)=a,\qquad q(b)=b,\qquad q'(a),q'(b)\le1. \tag{5.4} $$ If the constant coefficient is $c>0$, Section 4 makes $q'$ strictly convex in the gap. Continuity extends the chord comparison to its endpoints, giving $$ q'(t)<\frac{b-t}{b-a}q'(a)+\frac{t-a}{b-a}q'(b)\le1, \qquad a0. $$ The first term is nonnegative; strict convexity makes the second positive. Only continuity of $q'$ is needed at the ends. For example, a jump $\Delta\gamma$ at $s$ gives the one-sided identity $$ q''(s+)-q''(s-)=-2\Delta\gamma\,\mathbb E a(s,X_s)^3. $$ It follows by applying Itô's formula to $a^2$ and using continuity of its derivative moments on a compact strip. Taking $\gamma=0$ before $s=1/2$ and $\gamma=1/2$ afterward makes this jump strictly negative; the terminal Cole–Hopf solution has positive Hessian. Thus continuity of $q'$ does not license classical higher time derivatives across coefficient jumps. [OpenAI (2026a), proof of Corollary 6.4][fs-density]. If $c=0$, the separate heat argument in Section 4 makes $q'$ strictly increasing. Then $q'(t) There are two distinct possibilities at the left endpoint. If $(0,b)$ is a gap and $0\in S$, the preceding proof applies using the one-sided contact slope bound at zero. Because $(0,b)$ contains no mass, the support condition at zero forces an atom there and hence $c=\gamma(0)>0$. Its absence has not been proved at this stage. If instead the complementary component is $[0,b)$ with $0\notin S$, there is no mass anywhere in $[0,b)$. Thus $\gamma=0$ there. The identity $q(0)=0$ comes from zero-field symmetry, and the right endpoint gives $q(b)=b$, $q'(b)\le1$. Here $q''(t)>0$ for $00 \qquad(0\le a0$ is already impossible: either $h\le1$ everywhere, forcing $h\equiv1$ by its integral, or it attains an interior maximum above one, where $h'=0$ and $h''\le0$. This is an elementary deduction from these premises. Chen's conditional crossing theorem, with its own hypotheses, is of this form; §4 proves the stronger $q'''>0$ throughout a positive plateau, without a minimizer premise. See [Chen, arXiv:2607.18032v1, Proposition 4.2 and the proof of Proposition 4.3][chen26]. Neither statement supplies terminal contact at the excluded endpoint one.

**Lemma 2 (constant-interval curvature; [OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 5.1][FS]).** Let $\gamma\in\mathcal U$, with its associated diffusion and moment $q$. If $\gamma=c$ on an open interval $I\subset(0,1)$, called a plateau, then for $t\in I$ $$ q'''(t)\geq\frac{c^2}{1000}\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^4]>0 \quad\text{if }c>0. \tag{3} $$ If $c=0$, then $q''(t)=\mathbb E[\Phi_{xxx}(t,X_t)^2]>0$. Minimality is not a hypothesis of this lemma. Section 3 derives its moment polynomial and explains the integrated estimate imported from the source. **Proof of Theorem 1, assuming Lemma 2.** A complementary interval with two support endpoints admits two contact conditions; an initial interval without support at zero has coefficient zero; a terminal interval is handled here by a boundary estimate. Suppose $(\ell,r)$ is a support gap with endpoints in $S$ and $r<1$. The coefficient is a positive constant there: support at $\ell$ and absence of mass immediately to its right force $\mu_\gamma([0,\ell])>0$. Strict convexity of $q'$ and (2) give $$ q'(t)<\frac{r-t}{r-\ell}q'(\ell) +\frac{t-\ell}{r-\ell}q'(r)\leq1 \qquad(\ell0$, hence $q'(t)0$ and all $t$ sufficiently close to one. Two estimates produce this scale. The heat representation of the terminal value $|x|$ gives $1-u(t,x)^2\geq\kappa>0$ on $|x|\leq\sqrt{1-t}$. A transition-kernel comparison from a fixed earlier time gives a density $f_t(x)\geq m>0$ on the fixed window $|x|\leq1$, uniformly as $t\uparrow1$. Thus $$ 1-q(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}(1-u(t,x)^2)f_t(x)\,dx \geq2m\kappa\sqrt{1-t}. $$ The time-uniform density estimate, proved in Lemma 6.3, equations (6.6)–(6.7), is essential; pointwise positivity of each density would not suffice. For $h=1-t[long §5, “A shorter qualitative exclusion”](../long/reasoning-record.md#qualitative-terminal-gap). The boundary estimate retained here also describes the terminal behaviour of an arbitrary coefficient constant near one. The zero-coefficient heat argument and late-step variation have antecedents in [Chen, Handschy and Lerman (2018), Theorem 6 and its proof][CHL]. These cases exhaust the complement of the relatively closed set $S$. Consequently $S=[0,1)$, contact gives $q(t)=t$, and differentiation gives $\mathbb E a^2=1$, including the right-hand value at zero. Moreover, $\gamma(t_2)-\gamma(t_1)=\mu_\gamma((t_1,t_2])>0$. This proves Theorem 1 using the stated analytic inputs.

Adding a small atom at scale $s$ raises the cumulative function at
*every* later scale. It is always allowed: the total mass is not
fixed, so no compensating removal is required. Its direction is
$\eta(t)=\mathbf1_{[s,1)}(t)$, equal to zero before $s$ and one
from $s$ onward. Thus

$$
D\mathcal P(\gamma)[\mathbf1_{[s,1)}]
=\frac12\int_s^1(q(t)-t)\,dt=:\frac12G(s).
$$

For the candidate in Figure 1, adding $\varepsilon$ mass at $s=1/2$
creates a jump of height $\varepsilon$ there and raises the entire
remaining curve by $\varepsilon$. The coefficient changes only on
that tail, but its optimised value and feedback must be recomputed:
earlier starting states also face a changed future control problem. The
first-variation theorem accounts for this dependence. Its formula
has a tail integral because that is where the coefficient changes:
$G(s)/2$ is the marginal cost of placing mass at $s$. At a minimiser,
$G(s)\ge0$ for every $s<1$.

For the two weights in Section 2, the same accounting gives

$$
\int_0^1\gamma(t)(q(t)-t)\,dt
=2G(1/4)+G(3/4).
$$

Each weight is charged for its entire remaining tail. The $q$ and $G$
in this identity belong to that candidate; no optimality has been assumed.
Reducing both weights by a fraction $\varepsilon$ multiplies the
cumulative function by $1-\varepsilon$.

Suppose temporarily that this two-weight candidate minimised
$\mathcal P$. Addition would give two nonnegative costs,
$G(1/4)\ge0$ and $G(3/4)\ge0$, while the allowed reduction would give

$$
0\le-\frac12\bigl(2G(1/4)+G(3/4)\bigr).
$$

Both costs must be zero: their positive-weighted sum is nonnegative,
and the reduction forces it to be nonpositive. This is a necessary
condition under the temporary minimiser assumption, not a claim that
the two-weight candidate attains the minimum.

For a general minimiser, the same argument replaces the finite sum by
an integral. The direction $\eta=-\gamma$
is integrable, and $(1-\varepsilon)\gamma$ remains admissible for
$0\le\varepsilon\le1$. It scales all existing mass by the same
factor. For the continuous candidate in Figure 1, it multiplies the
two nonzero slopes and the plateau height by $1-\varepsilon$;
it works for diffuse mass as well as atoms.
The weighted-sum identity becomes

$$
0\le D\mathcal P(\gamma)[-\gamma]
=-\frac12\int_0^1\gamma(t)(q(t)-t)\,dt
=-\frac12\int_{[0,1)}G(s)\,\mu_\gamma(ds).
$$

The exchange of integration order is valid even if the total mass is
infinite. Its absolute integral is bounded by the area from Section 2:

$$
\int_{[0,1)}\int_s^1|q(t)-t|\,dt\,\mu_\gamma(ds)
=\int_0^1\gamma(t)|q(t)-t|\,dt
\le\int_0^1\gamma(t)\,dt<\infty.
$$

Since $G\ge0$, its integral must be zero. If $G$ were positive at a
support point, continuity would bound it below by a positive number
on a neighbourhood carrying positive mass, contradicting that zero
integral. Hence $G=0$ on the support. This is **contact**: the
nonnegative function touches zero there. The scaling argument is the
variational argument of [Chen, Proposition 3.2, equations (3.11)–(3.12)][chen-support],
applied with the integrable-direction formula above.

Scaling removes only mass that exists. In Figure 1, even the supported
point $1/4$ has no atom: intervals around it carry mass, but the point
itself does not. Subtracting $\varepsilon\delta_{1/4}$ would create a
downward jump. For $0<\varepsilon<1/4$ the cumulative values would
remain nonnegative, but the function would no longer be nondecreasing.
Support alone does not permit atom removal. We have proved contact
on the support, not that every zero of $G$ must carry mass.

### 5.2 Contact gives endpoint conditions

We need information about $q$ at the ends of a possible gap. An interior
support point $s$ is a minimum of $G$. Since
$G'(s)=s-q(s)$ and $G''(s)=1-q'(s)$, ordinary calculus gives

$$
q(s)=s,\qquad q'(s)\le1.
$$

At zero, if it belongs to the support, contact and symmetry give
$G(0)=q(0)=0$. If $q'(0)>1$, continuity would give $q'(t)>1$
for small positive $t$. Integration would then give $q(t)>t$, so
$G'(t)=t-q(t)<0$. Starting from $G(0)=0$, this would force $G(t)<0$,
a contradiction. Hence $q'(0)\le1$. This one-sided argument includes
an atom at zero.

### 5.3 Strict curvature creates an impossible integral

The support is relatively closed in $[0,1)$. Starting at a missing
point, enlarge its mass-free interval until it reaches support or a
boundary of the domain. Such a maximal interval has two
support endpoints, starts at zero outside the support, or reaches one.
We treat these three cases in order; the last includes empty support.

First suppose $(r,s)$ has both endpoints in the support, with
$0\le r<s<1$. Its constant height $c$ is necessarily positive:
for $t$ inside the gap, a small relative neighbourhood of $r$ lies in
$[0,t]$ and has positive mass, so $c=\mu_\gamma([0,t])>0$.
If $r=0$, this mass is an atom at zero. Contact imposes

$$
q(r)=r,\quad q(s)=s,\quad q'(r)\le1,\quad q'(s)\le1.
$$

The first two conditions require area $s-r$ under $q'$ across the gap.
A calculus model shows how strict convexity can prevent this. On the
earlier interval $[1/3,2/3]$, put $x=3t-1$ and consider the slope
$1-x(1-x)$. Its endpoints equal one, but

$$
\int_{1/3}^{2/3}[1-(3t-1)(2-3t)]\,dt
=\frac13\int_0^1[1-x(1-x)]\,dx=\frac5{18}.
$$

The missing area is $1/3-5/18=1/18$. This is a calculus model, not a
computed SK moment curve. The next input forces the actual $q'$ below
its endpoint chord in the same way.

**Strict-curvature input ([OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 5.1][support-curvature]).**
For any admissible coefficient equal to $c>0$ on an open interval,
its moment curve satisfies, strictly inside that interval,

$$
q'''(t)\ge\frac{c^2}{1000}\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^4]>0
\qquad(r<t<s).
$$

Section 7.3 explains how this sign is obtained after expectation.
The gap argument uses its strict sign; it does not use the particular
number $1/1000$.
The final inequality uses $a(t,x)>0$, proved by Gaussian smoothing
on the constant interval ([OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.3][support-regularity]);
convexity of $\Phi$ alone would only give $a\ge0$.
Because $q'''=(q')''$, the function $q'$ is strictly convex: between
two points its graph lies strictly below their joining chord.
The moment identity makes $q'$ continuous at the endpoints, even if
$\gamma$ jumps there; higher derivatives are needed only inside the gap.
Hence

$$
q'(t)<\frac{s-t}{s-r}q'(r)+\frac{t-r}{s-r}q'(s)\le1
\qquad(r<t<s).
$$

Integration gives $q(s)-q(r)<s-r$, contradicting contact. For the candidate in Section 2,
a minimising plateau on $(1/3,2/3)$ would require the same increment
to be both equal to and strictly less than $1/3$.
